_comment: b507 (2026-10-18) — the Wren Kids catalogue, in ONE place.
Read by src/routes/kids-games.js (the EY launcher and the child-profile card) and by
scripts/kids/build-site.py (the indexable per-game pages and the curriculum page).
The games' own code in public/kids/games/*.js repeats the curriculum line it shows the
child; everything a grown-up reads comes from here.
codes = fledge framework statement codes, resolved to ids per schema at write time.
elgs  = EYFS Early Learning Goal codes (eyfs_statutory_2026 in ladn.framework_statements).
nc    = the national curriculum reference for the KS1/KS2 games, which have no framework
table to point at. There is no official identifier scheme for NC statements —
gov.uk publishes the programmes of study as plain bullets — so this is prose, and
deliberately quotes the statutory wording. See the research note.
framework_in_force: EYFS statutory framework for group and school-based providers, in force 1 September 2026

games.title: Snap Count
games.subject: Early maths and number sense
games.plain: Subitising — recognising how many without counting.
games.mechanic: Spots flash on a plate for under a second, then the plate is covered and the child chooses how many. Dice faces first, then ten-frames, then scatters, then two separated groups so six reads as "four and two".
games.why: Subitising is the strongest early predictor of number fluency, and it is one of the few things a screen practises better than counters, because it needs the dots to appear and then disappear. A child who has time to count has not subitised.
games.levels: Five: dice to 3, dice to 5, ten-frame to 6, scatter to 6, two groups to 10.
games.at_home: Roll a dice and say the number before you count. Put three raisins on the table and ask "how many?" without counting. Flash fingers.

games.title: Ten Town Train
games.subject: Early maths and number sense
games.plain: The composition of numbers to 10 — "how many more to make ten?".
games.short: How many more to fill the train?
games.mechanic: Some carriages are full, some are empty. The child says how many more are needed, and then watches the train fill. Later levels turn it round: the train was filled, how many were full before?
games.why: The Reception goal is "a deep understanding of numbers to 10, including the composition of each number" — knowing 7 is 5 and 2, and 6 and 1, and 4 and 3. That is different from counting, and it is what becomes number bonds in Year 1. The empty carriages mean the answer is a picture before it is a numeral.
games.levels: Five: make 5, make 10, make 10 with bigger gaps, make any number to 10, and the inverse.
games.at_home: Five cups out and seven people — how many more? Count the gaps in an egg box. "We have three, how many more for six?"

games.title: Pattern Path
games.subject: Early maths and number sense
games.plain: Copying, continuing and completing repeating patterns.
games.mechanic: A line of stepping stones follows a pattern with one missing. Early levels put the gap at the end; later ones put it in the middle, which cannot be solved by copying the last thing you saw.
games.why: Spotting and continuing a pattern is an Early Learning Goal in its own right and the root of algebraic thinking — finding the unit of repeat, holding it, and applying it. Most pattern games never go past AB; this one climbs to ABB, ABC and AABB. Every element is a distinct shape as well as a distinct colour, so a colour-blind child plays the same game.
games.levels: Five: AB, ABB/AAB, ABC, AABB with the gap in the middle, and four-element units.
games.at_home: Lay out cup, spoon, cup, spoon and ask what comes next. Clap-clap-stamp. Thread beads. Say the pattern out loud together.

games.title: Rhyme Time
games.subject: Phonics and reading (the listening that comes first)
games.plain: Hearing rhyme and initial sounds — the oral skills that come before phonics.
games.mechanic: A picture and a spoken word. The child taps the picture that rhymes with it, or later the one that starts with the same sound, or the odd one out. No letters are shown until level 4.
games.why: This is phonological awareness, not phonics: it is entirely oral, and it is the strongest early predictor of how smoothly systematic synthetic phonics will go later. It deliberately does not teach letters and sounds — Wren Phonics does that properly and for free at phonics.getwren.co.uk, and this game links there.
games.levels: Five: rhyme with 2 pictures, rhyme with 3, odd one out, initial sounds, and mixed odd-one-out of 4.
games.at_home: Make up silly rhyming pairs at nappy time. "I spy something beginning with /s/" — the sound, not the letter name. Read rhyming books and stop before the rhyme so they fill it in.

games.title: Bond Rally
games.subject: KS1 maths: number bonds
games.nc: KS1 Mathematics. Year 1: "represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20". Year 2: "recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100".
games.plain: Number bonds and addition and subtraction facts to 20, practised for recall.
games.short: Number bonds and facts to 20, until they are automatic.
games.mechanic: Quick facts with four answers to choose from. Levels 1 and 2 show the bond as a part-whole bar first. Facts the child gets wrong are kept on the device and brought back round sooner.
games.why: "Fluently" is the word that matters: a child who works out 7 + 6 on their fingers every time has no working memory left for the actual problem. Facts become recall through retrieval practice spaced over time, not through more worked examples. There is deliberately no countdown clock — timing pressure is what makes fluency practice frightening for exactly the children who most need it.
games.levels: Five: bonds to 10 with the bar, bonds to 10, bonds to 20, subtraction within 20, missing number in any position.
games.at_home: One minute a day out loud beats twenty minutes once a week. "I say six, you say four." Count out ten and hide some — how many are hidden?

games.title: Spell Spotter
games.subject: KS1 English: spelling and SPaG
games.nc: KS1 English, Appendix 1 (Spelling): the Year 1 and Year 2 common exception words; -tch, -dge and -ck after a short vowel; adding -ing, -ed, -er and -est; plurals with -s and -es; contractions.
games.plain: Year 1 and Year 2 statutory spelling — common exception words and the named rules.
games.short: Spot the right spelling — and learn the rule.
games.mechanic: A real sentence with one word missing, read aloud, and three spellings to choose from. Get it wrong and you are told the rule, not just that you were wrong.
games.why: Every wrong spelling offered is an error children actually make — writen, becuase, cach, hopping-for-hoping. A randomly mangled word teaches nothing, because no child would ever have written it. And the rule is the part that transfers: "catch needs -tch after a short vowel" is useful next week; "wrong" is not.
games.levels: Five: Year 1 common exception words, Year 2 common exception words, -tch/-dge/-ck, adding -ing and -ed, plurals and contractions.
games.at_home: Ask them to tell you the rule back. Spot the pattern in a book — how many -tch words can you find on this page?

games.title: Tables Launch
games.subject: KS2 maths: times tables
games.nc: KS2 Mathematics. Year 4: "recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12". Year 2: the 2, 5 and 10 tables. Year 3: the 3, 4 and 8 tables. Rehearses the format of the statutory Multiplication Tables Check.
games.plain: Times tables to 12 × 12, weighted like the statutory Year 4 check.
games.short: Times tables, weighted the way the Year 4 check is.
games.mechanic: Multiplication and division facts, four answers to choose from. Level 5 is Check mode: typed on a keypad, six seconds a question, like the real thing.
games.why: Most tables apps drill 1×1 to 12×12 evenly, which spends most of a child's practice on facts they already know. The statutory check does not: it draws from the 2 to 12 tables (the 1× table is excluded) and emphasises the 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 tables because those are the hardest. This game weights its questions the same way, keeps a per-fact record on the device so wrong facts return sooner, and has no timer at all on levels 1 to 4.
games.levels: Five: the 2s, 5s and 10s; plus 3s, 4s and 8s; all tables to 12; division facts; Check mode.
games.at_home: Short and often. Pick one table a week and ask it out of order, including the division facts — 42 ÷ 6 is the same knowledge as 6 × 7.
games.note: This is practice in the official format, not an official practice tool. The Standards and Testing Agency's own try-it-out area sits behind a school sign-in.

games.title: Fraction Forest
games.subject: KS2 maths: fractions
games.nc: KS2 Mathematics. Year 3: "recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators". Year 4: equivalent fractions and fractions of a quantity. Year 5: compare and order fractions. Year 6: add and subtract fractions with the same denominator.
games.plain: Naming fractions, equivalence, fractions of an amount and comparing.
games.short: Fractions, with the picture before the symbol.
games.mechanic: Every question shows a divided bar first and the symbol second, and the child moves between them. By level 5 the bar is gone and only the numbers are left.
games.why: Fractions are where primary maths most often comes apart, and the reason is nearly always that the symbols arrived before the picture. Three-quarters is a number, not two numbers stacked up; 2/4 and 1/2 are the same number; "two thirds of 12" is a sharing action. All three are obvious with a bar in front of you and opaque without one.
games.levels: Five: name the shaded fraction, equivalence with bars, equivalence without, fraction of an amount, comparing and adding.
games.at_home: Cut things up and name the parts — half a sandwich, a quarter of an apple. Ask which is more, a third or a quarter, and then draw it.
